the structural classification for cleavage presented by Sorrell [1]. Figure 3 illustrates fluorite
cleavage. Several other crystals which are known to cleave with that geometry have had their
toughnesses measured and published. Table 5 summarizes those cleavage toughness results.
The three alkaline earth fluorides have toughnesses of the magnitudes typical for cleavage,
less than 1 MPa m 1/2. The toughness values decrease from Ca through Ba as do the elastic
moduli. It should be noted that the covalent bonding which is dominant in both silicon (Si) and
diamond (C) yields significantly higher cleavage toughnesses. This effect may be expected
from some of the previous discussions on charge and bond effects. The diamond (C) cleavage
toughnesses which are in the 3-5 MPa m 1/2 range are some of the highest reliable single
crystal cleavage toughness values which have ever been reported. As the high hardness of
diamond is well known, it is evident that coupling this high cleavage toughness value with the
extraordinarily high hardness value makes diamond almost ideal for the industrial abrasive

The passage does not provide MgO’s surface energy for the {100} cleavage plane, nor does it report the hardness of an MgO single crystal. Richard A. Schultz, Martin C. Jensen, and Richard C. Bradt. Single crystal cleavage of brittle materials. International Journal of Fracture, 65:291-312, Feb 1994. URL: https://doi.org/10.1007/bf00012370, doi:10.1007/bf00012370. This article has 126 citations and is from a peer-reviewed journal.

The excerpt discusses MgO in the context of cubic cleavage in ionic crystals with the NaCl structure. MgO cleaves on {100}, and its cleavage toughness is grouped with LiF as being approximately three times greater than the values for KBr and PbS. The text attributes this trend to MgO and LiF having smaller ions, stronger bonding, and higher elastic moduli than the compounds containing larger, more polarizable ions. It does not provide an explicit numerical MgO K_Ic value in the supplied pages, although it states that cubic-cleavage toughnesses are generally below 1 MPa m^1/2, with some approaching approximately 1 MPa m^1/2. The excerpt does not report MgO’s {100} surface energy, nor does it provide a hardness value for MgO single crystal. It also distinguishes MgO from pyrite and spinel, which have higher cubic-cleavage toughnesses of about 1 MPa m^1/2. Thus, the passage supports qualitative interpretation of MgO’s cleavage toughness and bonding-related trends, but numerical fracture toughness, surface-energy, and hardness values would need to be obtained from the article’s tables or other sources.

## pqac-00000029

From text 'boffi1976onthecleavage pages 1-5'.

S. Boffi and M. Ricci. On the cleavage energy of magnesium oxide. Materials Chemistry, 1:289-296, Dec 1976. URL: https://doi.org/10.1016/0390-6035(76)90030-4, doi:10.1016/0390-6035(76)90030-4. This article has 3 citations.

The excerpt concerns the theoretical cleavage energy and surface-energy framework for MgO, rather than reporting MgO fracture-toughness (KIc), hardness, or clearly tabulated numerical cleavage-energy values. Cleavage is modeled as a stress-induced phase transition: under uniaxial stress, the perfect lattice becomes unstable when the separation of planes reaches a critical displacement. The reversible work per unit area needed to reach this unstable configuration is denoted by γc, while an additional contribution γb is required for complete irreversible separation into two free surfaces. The model relates the critical displacement and cleavage work to interplanar force constants, phonon eigenfrequencies/eigenvectors, and a direction-dependent factor B(hkl). The [100] orientation is identified as the easy cleavage direction, and the text indicates anisotropy for other orientations, including [110]. MgO has the NaCl crystal structure and is treated using a modified breathing-shell model based on its elastic and phonon properties. However, the supplied pages do not provide a numerical value for KIc, a numerical {100} surface energy, or a hardness value for MgO single crystals. They also do not give the final numerical results, which appear to be discussed later in the article.

## 1. preuss2026stablecrackpropagation pages 1-3 (Context ID: pqac-00000035)

Stable crack propagation  in dislocation-engineered oxide visualized by double

cleavage drilled compression test


Oliver Preuß1a, Zhangtao Li2a, Enrico Bruder3, Philippe Carrez4, Yinan Cui2*, Jürgen Rödel1, Xufei
Fang5*

1Division Nonmetallic-Inorganic Materials, Department  of Materials and Earth Sciences, Technical
University of Darmstadt, Peter-Grünberg-Str. 2, 64287 Darmstadt, Germany

2Department of Engineering Mechanics, Tsinghua University, Mengminwei Building, Beijing 100084, P.R.
China

3Division Physical Metallurgy, Department of Materials and Earth Sciences, Technical University of
Darmstadt, Peter-Grünberg-Str. 2, 64287 Darmstadt, Germany

4Université Lille, CNRS, INRAE, Centrale Lille, UMR 8207—UMET—Unité Matériaux et Transformations,
Lille, France

5Institute of Applied Materials, Karlsruhe Institute of Technology, Kaiserstr. 12, 76131 Karlsruhe, Germany

a These authors contributed equally to this work.

* Corresponding authors: Yinan Cui: cyn@mail.tsinghua.edu.cn; Xufei Fang: xufei.fang@kit.edu



Abstract:

Understanding crack tip – dislocation interaction is critical for improving the fracture resistance of

semi-brittle materials like room-temperature plastically deformable ceramics. Here, we use a modified

double cleavage drilled compression (DCDC) specimen geometry, which facilitates stable crack

propagation, to achieve in situ observation of crack tip – dislocation interaction. MgO specimens,

furnished with dislocation-rich barriers, were employed to study how dislocations influence crack

propagation. Crack progression was clearly observed to decelerate within dislocation-rich regions,

slowing to 15% of its velocity as compared to the pristine crystal. Upon exiting these regions, cracks

reaccelerated until reaching the next dislocation-rich barrier. Coupled phase field and crystal plasticity

modeling replicates the experimental observations and provides mechanistic insight into crack tip –

dislocation interactions. The aligned experiment and simulation results underscore the robustness of

the technique and its potential to inform the design of more fracture-resistant ceramics via dislocations.



Keywords: Dislocation toughening; Stable crack growth; MgO; DCDC test; Dislocations in ceramics





                                           11. Introduction

The ability to resist crack growth via dislocations has led to the wide application of engineering metals

and alloys as structural materials. Phenomenologically, in these materials, the plastic deformation at

the crack tip involves dislocation emission, multiplication, and motion. This contributes to the shielding

and/or blunting of the crack tip, which inhibits and/or delays crack propagation, leading to a desirable

engineering property for damage-tolerant components. In ceramics, however, crack propagation is

energetically favoured over plastic deformation, which significantly limits their application in structural

components compared to metals [1]. In recent years, the promising development in dislocation-

engineered ceramics together with more discovered plastically deformable ceramics [2, 3] suggests

the possibility of dislocation-based toughening in ceramics even at room temperature. This  is

evidenced by the experimental observations in oxides and alkali halides [2, 4-9] that an area of high-

density dislocations can reduce the length of surface cracks induced by Vickers indentation, or

completely suppress crack formation. However, direct observation of the crack tip – dislocation at

mesoscale is still missing, primarily due to the challenge of engineering sufficiently large plastic zones

and achieving stable crack growth in ceramics. To enable the development of dislocation-toughened

ceramics,   it  is important  to pinpoint the underlying mechanisms by  directly observing crack

propagation in oxides with dislocations in a controlled manner.

For both metals and ceramics, several crack tip – dislocation interaction mechanisms have been

proposed to describe the origin of the dislocation toughening effect. This includes, for instance,

dislocation shielding (lowering of the local stress intensity factor by the presence of a suitably oriented

dislocation stress field) [4, 10]; dislocation emission (the crack front acts as a heterogeneous

dislocation source) [5, 11]; dislocation-based crack-tip blunting (an avalanche of emission events,

which leads to accumulating surface steps on the crack front changing the crack tip geometry) [12,

13]; and crack-tip plasticity (while propagating, the crack-tip stress field acts as a Peach-Köhler force

on pre-existing dislocations, effectively performing mechanical work) [14, 15]. Furthermore, pile-up

events of dislocations, such as the Zener-Stroh mechanism [16-18] or Cottrell mechanism [19], can

result in local stress concentration and eventually crack initiation. Provided that the cracks are initiated,

the core challenge for dislocation toughening shifts to crack tip – dislocation interaction during crack

propagation.

Experimentally, a direct, in situ method capable of tracking dislocations in the volume of interest much

larger than the process zone in a time-resolved manner is still missing for ceramics. Such a method

has to be developed to identify the prevalent mechanism in dislocation-based toughening for future

exploitation. Here, we summarize the most promising experimental approaches along this direction

in Table 1.

(TEM) observation by Appel et al. on single-crystal MgO at room temperature [23]. At a very slow

crack propagation rate (the source suggests a velocity of micrometers per hour), the formation of a

One of the most appealing approaches listed in Table 1 is the in situ transmission electron microscopy

(TEM) observation by Appel et al. on single-crystal MgO at room temperature [23]. At a very slow

crack propagation rate (the source suggests a velocity of micrometers per hour), the formation of a

dislocation-rich “plastic zone” (in the form of a process zone) in front of a loaded crack tip was



                                           3observed. The dislocations were generated by profuse multiplication in front of the crack tip. Based

on the configuration of the dislocations, the local stress intensity factor can be estimated to be ~0.55

MPa m0.5. A similar method was used later by Higashida et al. [5]  , who observed spontaneous

emission of mainly shielding-type screw dislocations from a mode-I crack tip in single-crystal MgO.

However, because of the thin TEM sample (in the range of hundreds of nm), the stress state during

in situ TEM experiments differs from those encountered in bulk samples, necessitating caution in the

extrapolation to bulk samples [24].

For ceramic materials, most testing geometries listed in Table 1 with notches and pre-cracks (to

circumvent crack initiation) obey the Griffith criterion [25]. This implies a rising driving force with

increasing crack length, which leads to unstable crack growth. When a crack reaches the propagation
criterion (𝐾𝐼 ≥ 𝐾𝐼𝐶) in brittle solids, it can accelerate to the speed of sound [26] or until the sample
breaks entirely, making the detailed observation impossible. Therefore, for detailed evolutionary
characterisation in brittle materials, stable crack growth with 𝜕𝐾𝐼 ≤0 is necessary, as the crack may
                                                            𝜕𝑎
be stopped at designated time/loading.

To achieve stable crack propagation in brittle solids, the double cleavage drilled compression (DCDC)

geometry was first used by Janssen in 1974 (compare Fig. 1A) [27]. This specimen geometry, tested

in a widely available compression setup, offers an inverse proportionality of stress intensity factor and
crack length (𝐾𝐼∝ 1 𝜕𝐾𝐼 < 0) [28]. This means that, for a given increase in applied stress, the crack                    𝑎, 𝜕𝑎
will extend a finite length and theoretically stop by itself in the loaded state without the need for

significant unloading. In other words, the crack growth in this experimental configuration is self-limiting.

With a step-wise increase in applied load, the crack length will increase step-wise. Further, the DCDC

geometry offers midplane crack stability and self-precracking [29]. The scalability of the DCDC test is

mostly limited in  brittle materials by the precise machining processes involved in the sample

manufacturing, mainly the achievable hole and notch sizes. The DCDC geometry also enables fatigue

testing in very brittle samples [30]. It is mostly used as a quantitative method to determine the fracture

toughness of brittle materials but also used to in situ observe crack deflection [31] and crack front

shapes [32, 33] when combined with X-ray methods or digital image correlation method.

Here, we adopt the DCDC test on single-crystal MgO to demonstrate stable crack propagation and

capture its interaction with the dislocation-rich areas at the mesoscale, for the first time. MgO is

chosen as a representative oxide that exhibits room-temperature dislocation  plasticity  in bulk

compression [34-36]. The test is carried out inside an SEM chamber to allow for concurrent in situ

observation of crack morphology and dislocation activity. Combined with electron channelling contrast

imaging (ECCI), new insight into crack tip – dislocation interaction in ductile oxides has been obtained.

Furthermore, a coupled crystal plasticity and phase field modelling is carried out for the DCDC test

with a focus on the crack tip – dislocation interactions to corroborate the experimental findings.


                                           42. Experimental procedure

2.1. Sample preparation

MgO single crystals (2 x 4 x 8 mm3) with well-polished surfaces were purchased from Alineason

Materials Technology GmbH  (Frankfurt am Main, Germany)  for the double cleavage  drilled

compression (DCDC) geometry given in Fig. 1A. All 8 mm long edges were chamfered to a 45° angle

using P4000 sandpaper and a fixture to hold the crystal at this angle to prevent stress concentrations

and edge flaws. The hole in the center was drilled using a water-cooled diamond hollow core drill

(Günther Diamantwerkzeuge e.K., Idar-Oberstein, Germany) with an outer diameter of 1.2 mm on a

conventional milling machine.

The pre-cracks were prepared using diamond wire that was threaded through the hole and tensioned

in a jigsaw. The opposing notches of ~0.5 mm depth were cut by hand with a sprayed water droplet

to facilitate the cutting. The sawed notches were later refined using a sharp razor blade and 1 µm

diamond paste. For reproducibility, three samples were prepared and tested under the same

conditions. Each sample contains 6 scratch tracks (orange strips in Fig. 1A), yielding in total 18 tracks

furnished with dislocations, acting as barriers right in front of the crack propagation path.





Figure 1. A) Double cleavage drilled compression (DCDC) sample geometry. The orange rectangles symbolize the positions
of the dislocation-rich scratch tracks. B) Differential Interference Contrast imaging of a single scratch track (between the two
white dashed lines) highlighting the slip traces. C) Electron channeling contrast imaging (ECCI) inside the scratch track as
marked by the purple box in B, revealing the high-density dislocations (white contrasts).

The dislocation-rich regions (i.e. the scratch tracks) were achieved using the cyclic Brinell scratching

method developed elsewhere  [37]. A hardened  steel  ball  of 2.5 mm diameter (Habu Hauck

Prüftechnik GmbH, Hochdorf-Assenheim, Germany) was used with a static load of 9.8 N (1 kgf) and

a velocity of 0.5 mm/s on a modified universal hardness tester (Finotest, Karl Frank GmbH, Weinheim,

Germany). The lateral movement was implemented by a spindle-driven stage (Thorlabs Inc., Newton,

NJ, USA) controlled by a custom LabVIEW programme. While the pristine MgO single crystals feature

a dislocation density of ~1012 m-2, the dislocation density increases with the number of passes during

scratching, with a saturation observed after about 10 passes [9]. Based on our previous work, to

achieve a high dislocation density (~1014 - 1015 m-2) in MgO to maximize the crack-arresting effect, 10

passes were repeated within each scratch track. The final scratch tracks have a width of ~120 µm, a



                                           5length of 3.5 mm, and are 0.5 mm apart from each other. It has been reported that the dislocations in

such scratch tracks on MgO penetrate as deep as the width of the scratch track due to the inherent

slip systems of the ½<110>{110} type being activated [9]. These slip planes either lie at an angle of

45° or 90° to the scratched surface. Introducing scratch tracks like this can lead to significant residual

stresses [9], which might influence the cracking behaviour.

The successful introduction of dislocations was confirmed by differential interference contrast (DIC)

imaging using an optical microscope (AxioImager 2, Carl Zeiss Microscopy GmbH, Jena, Germany)

and by electron channelling contrast imaging (ECCI) [38] inside a scanning electron microscope (SEM,

MIRA3-XM, Tescan, Brno, Czech Republic). In the optical microscope images, the slip traces are

visualized as vertical and horizontal lines in and around the scratch track (Fig. 1B). Employing ECCI,

the individual dislocations in the wear track appear as small white tails of high contrast (see Fig. 1C),

which allows estimation of dislocation density. Here, the mean distance between dislocations in the

black areas is roughly 50 nm, which translates into an estimated dislocation density of 4x1014 m-2 [9],

which is 2 orders of magnitude higher than that in the surrounding reference material.

Stubbs4, Peter J. Eng4,5, Anna K. Wanhala4, Jeffrey D. Einkauf3, Matthew G. Boebinger6, Andrew

  *Corresponding Author: phone: 718-997-3338; email: jacquelyn.bracco@qc.cuny.edu





  1 KEYWORDS

  Direct air capture of CO2, carbon removal, interfacial chemistry, MgO


 ABSTRACT


Mineralization by MgO is an attractive potential strategy for direct air capture (DAC) of CO2 due

to its tendency to form carbonate phases upon exposure to water and CO2. Hydration of MgO

during this process is typically assumed to not be rate limiting, even at ambient temperatures.

However, surface passivation by hydrated phases likely reduces CO2 capture capacity. Here, we

examine the initial hydration reactions that occur on MgO(100) surfaces to determine if they could

potentially impact CO2 uptake. We first used atomic force microscopy (AFM) to explore changes

in reaction layers in water (pH = 6 and 12) and MgO saturated solution (pH = 11) and found the

reaction layers on MgO are heterogeneous and non-uniform. To determine how relative humidity

(R.H.) affects reactivity, we reacted samples at room temperature in nominally dry N2 (~11-12%

R.H.) for up to 12 hours, humid (>95% R.H.) N2 for 5, 10, and 15 minutes, and in air at 33% and

75% R.H. for 8 days. X-ray reflectivity and electron microscopy analysis of the samples reveals

that hydrated phases form rapidly upon exposure to humid air, but growth of the hydrated reaction

layer slows after its initial formation. Reaction layer thickness is strongly correlated with relative

humidity, with denser reaction layers forming in 75% R.H. as compared with 33% R.H. or

nominally dry N2. The reaction layers are likely amorphous or poorly crystalline based on grazing

incidence x-ray diffraction measurements. After exposure to 75% R.H. in air for 8 days, the

reaction layer increases in density as compared to the sample reacted in humid N2 for 5-15 minutes.

This may represent an initial step towards crystallization of the reaction layer. Overall, high

relative humidity favors the formation of a hydrated, disordered layer on MgO. Based on our



  2results DAC in a location with higher relative humidity will be favorable, but growth may slow

significantly from initial rates even on short timescales, presumably due to surface passivation.


 INTRODUCTION


The latest Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change Synthesis Report highlights the need for

negative emissions strategies, such as direct air capture (DAC) of CO2 for subsequent storage or

utilization, to meet net-zero greenhouse gas emissions targets.1 Presently, the majority of DAC

plants use liquid amines as absorbents for the CO2,2 but mineralization is also a potentially

promising technique.3 Mineralization strategies include saline mineralization,4, 5 conversion of

silicate minerals,6 and weathering of silicate or oxide minerals.7-11 However, there are challenges

associated with mineralization strategies, for example, passivation layers inhibiting CO2 uptake

can form on silicate minerals due to polymerization of silicic acid during dissolution and formation

of silica rich leached layers.7, 12-16 DAC with alkaline metal oxide minerals, such as CaO and MgO,

may be cheaper and more feasible compared to other mineral systems if a mineral looping process

is used. In this approach, metal carbonates are calcined to form metal oxides that are typically

amorphous and highly reactive. These metal oxides react with CO2 in the atmosphere at ambient

conditions for a designated time period to form metal carbonates. They are then calcined again to

separate the captured CO2, which can then be either sequestered in the subsurface,2, 17 or utilized

to make cements18 or plastics19, while the MgO or CaO material is reused for further CO2 capture.

Calcining of MgO for CO2 separation requires lower temperatures (350-600C20) than calcining

of CaO (~650-1000C)21-23 and therefore may be more cost effective. Industrially, MgO is

produced by two main methods: (1) calcination of magnesium-containing minerals,24 e.g. dolomite





  3or magnesite and (2) from brine or seawater, in which Mg(OH)2 is precipitated which is then

calcined. Depending on calcining temperature, the reactivity of the resulting MgO varies.25

  Currently, the technology readiness level (TRL) for ambient weathering of alkali metal oxides

as a strategy for DAC is 4 in a recent cost analysis by Young et al., 2023, which classifies this

technology as being in a very early stage of development.26 In the case of lower TRLs for CO2

capture technologies, developing accurate estimations of feasibility is crucial as these influence

which technologies are chosen for progression and direct approaches (i.e., extrapolation) can

underestimate costs.27 As such, assumptions on rate limiting steps can have an outsized influence

on cost estimates. In the analysis of McQueen and coworkers,17  it is assumed that brucite

(Mg(OH)2) forms rapidly and its dissolution rate is rate limiting and the carbonate product is

magnesite (MgCO3),  rather  than amorphous  or  hydrated  carbonate  phases. With  these

assumptions, mineral looping with MgO is expected to be inexpensive ($46-159/ton of CO2) and

could potentially be used to sequester up to 2-3 Gtons CO2/year.17 However, the extent and rate of

the reaction of MgO with CO2 is poorly constrained under conditions relevant for DAC,28 such as

the dependence on temperature and varying relative humidity, which makes it challenging to

evaluate how cost effective MgO is for DAC relative to CaO or other techniques.

  Recent studies have examined the impact of various parameters on carbonation reactions for

DAC during ambient weathering of MgO. For example, a recent study by Rausis  et  al.

demonstrated that under ambient conditions the supply of CO2 to MgO particles is rate limiting.28

There is also evidence that hydrated magnesium carbonate phases may passivate Mg(OH)2

surfaces and will thus limit carbonation reaction rates, especially at high temperatures.29 Growth

of amorphous magnesium carbonate occurs even more readily at lower temperatures, such as those

used during ambient weathering conditions, causing surface passivation MgO surfaces.30 At least



  4six different hydrated Mg-carbonate phases with varying water contents are known.31, 32 Under

ambient temperatures and CO2 partial pressures, precipitation of hydrated magnesium carbonate

phases, such as dypingite (Mg5(CO3)4(OH2)~5H2O), is expected but more crucially, Rausis and

coworkers were not able to find evidence of magnesite formation.28 This may be problematic for

DAC as hydrated phase formation leads to less CO2 uptake than would occur  if MgCO3

precipitates, based on the crystal volume per CO2 molecule. Recent work by Weber et  al.,

confirmed hydrated magnesium carbonate phases form on MgO surfaces on samples reacted in air

for months to years, with the reaction rate slowing over time due to armoring of the surface by

passivation layers.33 Based on diffusion modeling, the majority of the reaction occurs within the

first two years.33 Rausis et al., had suggested that 90% carbonation of MgO will require 5-27 years,

assuming little change in reaction rates over long periods of time.28 However, Weber and coauthors

observed that even after 27 years, 90% carbonation is not reached, suggesting passivation has a

significant impact.33 Knowledge of formation conditions for the hydrated MgO phases is therefore

critical for a successful DAC strategy.

  While there have been studies on longer term (days to months to years) formation of hydrated

The excerpt describes cleaving MgO or (Mg,Fe)O single crystals immediately before measurements to remove the passivated outer layer and expose a fresh mineral surface. {"answer": "## Cleavage of Bulk Single-Crystal MgO Along {100}: Techniques, Reliability, Failure Modes, and Quantitative Properties

### Background

Magnesium oxide (MgO, periclase) crystallizes in the NaCl-type rock-salt structure (space group Fm3̅m), which provides three mutually perpendicular families of {100} cleavage planes (pqac-00000009, pqac-00000013). Because each {100} plane is electrostatically neutral—alternating cations and anions across the surface—it satisfies the charge-neutrality exclusionary criterion for cleavage in ionic crystals, whereas {111} planes are non-neutral and cannot cleave (pqac-00000016). The {100} cleavage toughness of MgO is 0.81 MPa·m^(1/2), derived from Gilman's (1960) measurements and tabulated by Schultz, Jensen, and Bradt (1994) among other cubic structures (pqac-00000022, pqac-00000026). This is roughly three times larger than the cleavage toughness of softer halide crystals such as KBr (0.12 MPa·m^(1/2)) or NaCl (0.17 MPa·m^(1/2)), but still well below 1 MPa·m^(1/2) and therefore in the regime where cleavage proceeds readily once an adequate crack is initiated (pqac-00000025, pqac-00000027).

The following table summarizes the key quantitative properties governing {100} cleavage of single-crystal MgO:

<artifact id="artifact-00"/>

The experimental {100} surface energies reported in the literature cluster around 1.0–1.2 J/m². Gilman (1960) measured 1.20 J/m² by monocrystal cleavage, while Westwood and Goldheim (1963) obtained values in the range 1.04–1.15 J/m² (pqac-00000034, pqac-00000047). The literature average of six published values on {100} is 1.26 J/m² (pqac-00000048). Boffi and Ricci (1976) calculated a theoretical cleavage surface energy of 890 erg/cm² (0.89 J/m²) for {100}, noting that the predicted easy-cleavage direction and energy magnitude are consistent with experiment (pqac-00000034, pqac-00000047). The comparison of surface energy values from multiple authors is shown in the figure below (pqac-00000051).

---

### (1) Razor Blade / Chisel Technique and Reliability for a 10 × 10 × 10 mm Cube

The technique described by SPI Supplies—placing a single-edge razor blade or chisel on a {100} face, aligned parallel to a cube edge, and tapping it with a small hammer—is consistent with widespread laboratory practice for cleaving MgO. Multiple research groups have adopted a nearly identical procedure. Weber et al. (2023) state that "MgO single crystals were freshly cleaved using a razor blade" just before experiments, with loose debris then removed by blowing nitrogen gas over the surface (pqac-00000041). Bracco et al. (2024) and Meneses et al. (2025) independently describe the same procedure, cleaving MgO with a razor blade immediately before measurements, sometimes inside a glovebag or glovebox to control atmosphere (pqac-00000040).

In the primary research literature, Futagami and Akashi (1973) cleaved MgO blocks approximately 7 × 7 × 7 mm³ at room temperature using "a chisel fitted with a sharp knife edge." The knife edge was aligned along [001] on the (010) face, and a blow was applied in the [010] direction, producing (100) cleavage slabs approximately 1 mm thick (pqac-00000000, pqac-00000042). Langdon and Pask (1968) noted that MgO can be cleaved on a soft pad of tissue paper to produce surfaces free of micro-cracks (pqac-00000001).

**Reliability for a 10 × 10 × 10 mm cube:** The razor-blade-and-tap method is generally reliable for producing {100} cleavage in MgO cubes of this size, because (a) MgO's {100} cleavage toughness of 0.81 MPa·m^(1/2) is low enough for a sharp blade impact to initiate unstable fracture (pqac-00000026), and (b) once initiated, the crack is rapidly redirected by the crystal structure onto the preferred {100} cleavage plane, even if the blade is not perfectly aligned (pqac-00000018). However, the outcome is not guaranteed to be a single, atomically flat plane. Common complications include chipping at the blade contact point, cleavage steps from multiple crack origins, and potential deviation of the crack front from the intended direction (pqac-00000005, pqac-00000020). For a 10 mm cube cleaved in half, the geometry is favorable because the crack path length is modest relative to the crystal size. Attempting to take a thin slab (< 1 mm) from the edge is considerably more challenging and prone to shattering or multiple fracture.

---

### (2) Recommended Tool, Impact, Support, and Geometry

**Tool:** A sharp, single-edge razor blade or a chisel with a fine knife edge is the standard tool. The razor blade must be fresh and sharp, as MgO has a Mohs hardness of 5.5 (pqac-00000030) and a Knoop hardness of approximately 11 GPa (pqac-00000045), meaning it can rapidly dull a blade. Futagami and Akashi specifically used "a chisel fitted with a sharp knife edge" (pqac-00000000). Preuss et al. (2026) refined diamond-wire-sawn notches using "a sharp razor blade and 1 µm diamond paste" to prepare pre-cracks in MgO DCDC specimens, demonstrating that a razor blade is adequate for creating fine starter notches (pqac-00000036).

**Impact:** A light but sharp tap is preferable to a heavy blow. MgO is brittle with a low cleavage toughness (0.81 MPa·m^(1/2)), so only modest force is needed to nucleate a crack; excessive force risks shattering the crystal or generating excessive plastic deformation beneath the blade (pqac-00000008, pqac-00000012). Futagami and Akashi applied a single blow that generated a rapidly propagating cleavage crack (pqac-00000000). A small jeweler's hammer or similar light instrument is appropriate.

**Support:** The crystal should be placed on a compliant substrate rather than a rigid anvil. Langdon and Pask (1968) specifically recommend cleaving MgO "on a soft pad of tissue paper" to prevent surface micro-cracking on the bottom face and unwanted fracture from reflected stress waves (pqac-00000001). A hard anvil can generate Hertzian contact damage, introduce reflected tensile waves, and degrade the cleavage surface.

**Geometry:** Splitting the crystal approximately in half is the most reliable geometry. For a 10 × 10 × 10 mm cube, the blade should be placed at the midpoint of one face, aligned along a <100> direction. Taking thin slabs near an edge becomes increasingly difficult below about 1 mm thickness, which was the minimum slab thickness reported by Futagami and Akashi for 7 mm cubes (pqac-00000000). MgO's relatively high cleavage toughness compared to other NaCl-structure crystals means that thinner slabs require more precise initiation and are prone to multiple fracture.

---

### (3) Documented Causes of Failed or Poor Cleaves

Multiple mechanisms have been documented in the primary literature as causes of imperfect cleavage in MgO:

**Plastic deformation and {110}⟨1̅10⟩ dislocation slip under the blade.** MgO's primary room-temperature slip system is {110}⟨1̅10⟩ (pqac-00000009, pqac-00000006). The concentrated stress field beneath the blade or chisel can activate slip on these planes before the crack propagates, generating dislocations that absorb energy and interfere with clean cleavage. Futagami and Akashi (1973) observed that cleavage activates 45° slip bands on (110) planes, and that fresh edge dislocations with ½⟨110⟩-type Burgers vectors are nucleated near the fracture surface, especially at large cleavage steps (pqac-00000012, pqac-00000008). The plastic work contribution at room temperature is estimated to be only a few percent of the intrinsic surface energy but can become significant when crack velocity changes (pqac-00000008).

**Dislocation nucleation and multiplication at the crack front.** Concentrated stress at the crack tip nucleates fresh dislocations rather than merely mobilizing pre-existing ones. These dislocations form long parallel arrays near major cleavage steps and can slow or arrest crack propagation (pqac-00000005). Preuss et al. (2026) directly observed cracks decelerating to 15% of their initial velocity when entering dislocation-rich regions in MgO (pqac-00000035).

**Cleavage steps from multiple crack origins.** When cracks initiate at different microscopic sites and propagate simultaneously on slightly displaced parallel planes, one crack front thrusts into the other, producing large cleavage steps. River lines on the fracture surface indicate changing propagation paths (pqac-00000005, pqac-00000002).

**Kink bands and Stroh cracks.** Nonhomogeneous deformation creates kink bands that act as crack origins. Stroh cracks form when piled-up edge dislocations generate sufficient stress concentration at a barrier, nucleating cracks on conjugate {110} slip planes rather than on the intended {100} cleavage plane (pqac-00000006, pqac-00000011).

**Crack deflection by slip bands.** Propagating cleavage cracks are slowed when cutting through regions densely populated by screw dislocations; slip bands can impede crack growth in certain directions and redirect the crack path. A secondary crack bounded by slip bands may reorient before entering the cleavage plane (pqac-00000010).

**Sub-grain boundaries.** Bulk MgO crystals typically contain grown-in dislocation densities of approximately 10^6 cm⁻² organized into sub-grains of roughly 1 mm² (pqac-00000012). Although Futagami and Akashi (1973) found no clear relationship between observed fresh-dislocation regions and sub-grain boundaries despite many grown-in dislocations in those boundaries (pqac-00000005), sub-grain boundaries can tilt the local lattice orientation and potentially cause crack deflection at the boundary.

**Surface damage and micro-cracks.** Pre-existing edge micro-cracks or handling damage on the crystal surface provide uncontrolled fracture origins. Even cracks smaller than the critical Griffith size can grow once slip occurs and lead to fracture from unintended locations (pqac-00000017, pqac-00000011). This is why cleaving on a soft pad is important (pqac-00000001).

**Dull blade.** MgO's Mohs hardness of 5.5 and Knoop hardness of ~11 GPa mean that a dull blade distributes force over a larger area, promotes plastic deformation over fracture initiation, and increases the likelihood of crushing rather than cleaving. A fresh, sharp edge is essential.

---

### (4) Effect of Pre-Scoring or Sawing a Notch on Cleavage Initiation

Pre-scoring or sawing a guide notch generally **helps** cleavage initiation in MgO by providing a controlled stress concentrator at the desired location and orientation. Schultz et al. (1994) state that fracture toughness measurements on single crystals are commonly made "by some form of indentation pre-cracking, or by utilizing guide notches to force the incipient crack to initiate on the crystallographic plane of interest." After extending only a short distance, propagating cracks in single crystals are redirected by the crystal structure onto the preferred cleavage plane (pqac-00000018).

Langdon and Pask (1968) demonstrated that surface flaws serve as fracture origins in MgO: damaged or cleaved surfaces produced fracture origins at the crystal periphery coincident with surface flaws. Conversely, polishing away such cracks increased ductility five- to tenfold (pqac-00000017). This confirms that a deliberately introduced notch or score lowers the stress needed for cleavage initiation.

In recent work, Preuss et al. (2026) prepared MgO DCDC test specimens by first drilling a central hole, then cutting opposing notches (~0.5 mm deep) using diamond wire threaded through the hole. The sawed notches were subsequently refined using a sharp razor blade and 1 µm diamond paste to create well-defined pre-cracks (pqac-00000036). This two-step approach—coarse sawing followed by blade-refinement—represents best practice for controlled crack initiation in MgO.

**Caveats:** While a notch assists initiation, sawing introduces a damage zone containing dislocations and micro-cracks in the near-surface region (pqac-00000005). The width and depth of this damage zone depend on the cutting method and speed. For simple laboratory cleavage (as opposed to fracture-mechanics testing), a light score with a sharp blade or diamond scribe along the intended {100} cleavage line, followed by a tap with a sharp blade at that score, is preferable to deep sawing. The score should be shallow enough to avoid introducing heavy subsurface plasticity but deep enough to serve as a reliable stress concentrator. Futagami and Akashi's observation that the crack front can deviate from the nominal loading direction (pqac-00000020) underscores that even with a guide notch, the cleavage path is not guaranteed to be perfectly straight, particularly in crystals with high grown-in dislocation densities or sub-grain structure.

---

### Summary of Practical Recommendations

For cleaving a 10 × 10 × 10 mm MgO single crystal along {100} at room temperature in air:

1. Use a fresh, sharp single-edge razor blade or fine-edged chisel.
2. Place the crystal on a compliant pad (tissue paper or soft polymer mat).
3. Align the blade edge precisely along a ⟨100⟩ direction on the target {100} face.
4. Optionally pre-score lightly with a diamond scribe along the intended cleavage line to guide initiation.
5. Apply a single, light, sharp tap with a small hammer.
6. Splitting approximately in half is more reliable than attempting thin slabs; slabs thinner than ~1 mm become increasingly difficult.
7. Remove loose debris by blowing with dry nitrogen or compressed air (pqac-00000041).

The method is broadly reliable for MgO given its low cleavage toughness (0.81 MPa·m^(1/2)) and perfect {100} cleavage, but the user should expect occasional cleavage steps, river lines, and minor surface damage, particularly if the blade is dull, the crystal contains sub-grain boundaries, or the impact force is excessive."}

{"answer": "## Cleavage of Bulk Single-Crystal MgO Along {100}: Techniques, Reliability, Failure Modes, and Quantitative Properties

### Background

Magnesium oxide (MgO, periclase) crystallizes in the NaCl-type rock-salt structure (space group Fm3̅m), which provides three mutually perpendicular families of {100} cleavage planes (pqac-00000009, pqac-00000013). Because each {100} plane is electrostatically neutral—alternating cations and anions across the surface—it satisfies the charge-neutrality exclusionary criterion for cleavage in ionic crystals, whereas {111} planes are non-neutral and cannot cleave (pqac-00000016). The {100} cleavage toughness of MgO is 0.81 MPa·m^(1/2), derived from Gilman's (1960) measurements and tabulated by Schultz, Jensen, and Bradt (1994) among other cubic structures (pqac-00000022, pqac-00000026). This is roughly three times larger than the cleavage toughness of softer halide crystals such as KBr (0.12 MPa·m^(1/2)) or NaCl (0.17 MPa·m^(1/2)), but still well below 1 MPa·m^(1/2) and therefore in the regime where cleavage proceeds readily once an adequate crack is initiated (pqac-00000025, pqac-00000027).

The following table summarizes the key quantitative properties governing {100} cleavage of single-crystal MgO:

<artifact id="artifact-00"/>

The experimental {100} surface energies reported in the literature cluster around 1.0–1.2 J/m². Gilman (1960) measured 1.20 J/m² by monocrystal cleavage, while Westwood and Goldheim (1963) obtained values in the range 1.04–1.15 J/m² (pqac-00000034, pqac-00000047). The literature average of six published values on {100} is 1.26 J/m² (pqac-00000048). Boffi and Ricci (1976) calculated a theoretical cleavage surface energy of 890 erg/cm² (0.89 J/m²) for {100}, noting that the predicted easy-cleavage direction and energy magnitude are consistent with experiment (pqac-00000034, pqac-00000047). The comparison of surface energy values from multiple authors is shown in the figure below (pqac-00000051).

---

### (1) Razor Blade / Chisel Technique and Reliability for a 10 × 10 × 10 mm Cube

The technique described by SPI Supplies—placing a single-edge razor blade or chisel on a {100} face, aligned parallel to a cube edge, and tapping it with a small hammer—is consistent with widespread laboratory practice for cleaving MgO. Multiple research groups have adopted a nearly identical procedure. Weber et al. (2023) state that "MgO single crystals were freshly cleaved using a razor blade" just before experiments, with loose debris then removed by blowing nitrogen gas over the surface (pqac-00000041). Bracco et al. (2024) and Meneses et al. (2025) independently describe the same procedure, cleaving MgO with a razor blade immediately before measurements, sometimes inside a glovebag or glovebox to control atmosphere (pqac-00000040).

In the primary research literature, Futagami and Akashi (1973) cleaved MgO blocks approximately 7 × 7 × 7 mm³ at room temperature using "a chisel fitted with a sharp knife edge." The knife edge was aligned along [001] on the (010) face, and a blow was applied in the [010] direction, producing (100) cleavage slabs approximately 1 mm thick (pqac-00000000, pqac-00000042). Langdon and Pask (1968) noted that MgO can be cleaved on a soft pad of tissue paper to produce surfaces free of micro-cracks (pqac-00000001).

**Reliability for a 10 × 10 × 10 mm cube:** The razor-blade-and-tap method is generally reliable for producing {100} cleavage in MgO cubes of this size, because (a) MgO's {100} cleavage toughness of 0.81 MPa·m^(1/2) is low enough for a sharp blade impact to initiate unstable fracture (pqac-00000026), and (b) once initiated, the crack is rapidly redirected by the crystal structure onto the preferred {100} cleavage plane, even if the blade is not perfectly aligned (pqac-00000018). However, the outcome is not guaranteed to be a single, atomically flat plane. Common complications include chipping at the blade contact point, cleavage steps from multiple crack origins, and potential deviation of the crack front from the intended direction (pqac-00000005, pqac-00000020). For a 10 mm cube cleaved in half, the geometry is favorable because the crack path length is modest relative to the crystal size. Attempting to take a thin slab (< 1 mm) from the edge is considerably more challenging and prone to shattering or multiple fracture.

---

### (2) Recommended Tool, Impact, Support, and Geometry

**Tool:** A sharp, single-edge razor blade or a chisel with a fine knife edge is the standard tool. The razor blade must be fresh and sharp, as MgO has a Mohs hardness of 5.5 (pqac-00000030) and a Knoop hardness of approximately 11 GPa (pqac-00000045), meaning it can rapidly dull a blade. Futagami and Akashi specifically used "a chisel fitted with a sharp knife edge" (pqac-00000000). Preuss et al. (2026) refined diamond-wire-sawn notches using "a sharp razor blade and 1 µm diamond paste" to prepare pre-cracks in MgO DCDC specimens, demonstrating that a razor blade is adequate for creating fine starter notches (pqac-00000036).

**Impact:** A light but sharp tap is preferable to a heavy blow. MgO is brittle with a low cleavage toughness (0.81 MPa·m^(1/2)), so only modest force is needed to nucleate a crack; excessive force risks shattering the crystal or generating excessive plastic deformation beneath the blade (pqac-00000008, pqac-00000012). Futagami and Akashi applied a single blow that generated a rapidly propagating cleavage crack (pqac-00000000). A small jeweler's hammer or similar light instrument is appropriate.

**Support:** The crystal should be placed on a compliant substrate rather than a rigid anvil. Langdon and Pask (1968) specifically recommend cleaving MgO "on a soft pad of tissue paper" to prevent surface micro-cracking on the bottom face and unwanted fracture from reflected stress waves (pqac-00000001). A hard anvil can generate Hertzian contact damage, introduce reflected tensile waves, and degrade the cleavage surface.

**Geometry:** Splitting the crystal approximately in half is the most reliable geometry. For a 10 × 10 × 10 mm cube, the blade should be placed at the midpoint of one face, aligned along a <100> direction. Taking thin slabs near an edge becomes increasingly difficult below about 1 mm thickness, which was the minimum slab thickness reported by Futagami and Akashi for 7 mm cubes (pqac-00000000). MgO's relatively high cleavage toughness compared to other NaCl-structure crystals means that thinner slabs require more precise initiation and are prone to multiple fracture.

---

### (3) Documented Causes of Failed or Poor Cleaves

Multiple mechanisms have been documented in the primary literature as causes of imperfect cleavage in MgO:

**Plastic deformation and {110}⟨1̅10⟩ dislocation slip under the blade.** MgO's primary room-temperature slip system is {110}⟨1̅10⟩ (pqac-00000009, pqac-00000006). The concentrated stress field beneath the blade or chisel can activate slip on these planes before the crack propagates, generating dislocations that absorb energy and interfere with clean cleavage. Futagami and Akashi (1973) observed that cleavage activates 45° slip bands on (110) planes, and that fresh edge dislocations with ½⟨110⟩-type Burgers vectors are nucleated near the fracture surface, especially at large cleavage steps (pqac-00000012, pqac-00000008). The plastic work contribution at room temperature is estimated to be only a few percent of the intrinsic surface energy but can become significant when crack velocity changes (pqac-00000008).

**Dislocation nucleation and multiplication at the crack front.** Concentrated stress at the crack tip nucleates fresh dislocations rather than merely mobilizing pre-existing ones. These dislocations form long parallel arrays near major cleavage steps and can slow or arrest crack propagation (pqac-00000005). Preuss et al. (2026) directly observed cracks decelerating to 15% of their initial velocity when entering dislocation-rich regions in MgO (pqac-00000035).

**Cleavage steps from multiple crack origins.** When cracks initiate at different microscopic sites and propagate simultaneously on slightly displaced parallel planes, one crack front thrusts into the other, producing large cleavage steps. River lines on the fracture surface indicate changing propagation paths (pqac-00000005, pqac-00000002).

**Kink bands and Stroh cracks.** Nonhomogeneous deformation creates kink bands that act as crack origins. Stroh cracks form when piled-up edge dislocations generate sufficient stress concentration at a barrier, nucleating cracks on conjugate {110} slip planes rather than on the intended {100} cleavage plane (pqac-00000006, pqac-00000011).

**Crack deflection by slip bands.** Propagating cleavage cracks are slowed when cutting through regions densely populated by screw dislocations; slip bands can impede crack growth in certain directions and redirect the crack path. A secondary crack bounded by slip bands may reorient before entering the cleavage plane (pqac-00000010).

**Sub-grain boundaries.** Bulk MgO crystals typically contain grown-in dislocation densities of approximately 10^6 cm⁻² organized into sub-grains of roughly 1 mm² (pqac-00000012). Although Futagami and Akashi (1973) found no clear relationship between observed fresh-dislocation regions and sub-grain boundaries despite many grown-in dislocations in those boundaries (pqac-00000005), sub-grain boundaries can tilt the local lattice orientation and potentially cause crack deflection at the boundary.

**Surface damage and micro-cracks.** Pre-existing edge micro-cracks or handling damage on the crystal surface provide uncontrolled fracture origins. Even cracks smaller than the critical Griffith size can grow once slip occurs and lead to fracture from unintended locations (pqac-00000017, pqac-00000011). This is why cleaving on a soft pad is important (pqac-00000001).

**Dull blade.** MgO's Mohs hardness of 5.5 and Knoop hardness of ~11 GPa mean that a dull blade distributes force over a larger area, promotes plastic deformation over fracture initiation, and increases the likelihood of crushing rather than cleaving. A fresh, sharp edge is essential.

---

### (4) Effect of Pre-Scoring or Sawing a Notch on Cleavage Initiation

Pre-scoring or sawing a guide notch generally **helps** cleavage initiation in MgO by providing a controlled stress concentrator at the desired location and orientation. Schultz et al. (1994) state that fracture toughness measurements on single crystals are commonly made "by some form of indentation pre-cracking, or by utilizing guide notches to force the incipient crack to initiate on the crystallographic plane of interest." After extending only a short distance, propagating cracks in single crystals are redirected by the crystal structure onto the preferred cleavage plane (pqac-00000018).

Langdon and Pask (1968) demonstrated that surface flaws serve as fracture origins in MgO: damaged or cleaved surfaces produced fracture origins at the crystal periphery coincident with surface flaws. Conversely, polishing away such cracks increased ductility five- to tenfold (pqac-00000017). This confirms that a deliberately introduced notch or score lowers the stress needed for cleavage initiation.

In recent work, Preuss et al. (2026) prepared MgO DCDC test specimens by first drilling a central hole, then cutting opposing notches (~0.5 mm deep) using diamond wire threaded through the hole. The sawed notches were subsequently refined using a sharp razor blade and 1 µm diamond paste to create well-defined pre-cracks (pqac-00000036). This two-step approach—coarse sawing followed by blade-refinement—represents best practice for controlled crack initiation in MgO.

**Caveats:** While a notch assists initiation, sawing introduces a damage zone containing dislocations and micro-cracks in the near-surface region (pqac-00000005). The width and depth of this damage zone depend on the cutting method and speed. For simple laboratory cleavage (as opposed to fracture-mechanics testing), a light score with a sharp blade or diamond scribe along the intended {100} cleavage line, followed by a tap with a sharp blade at that score, is preferable to deep sawing. The score should be shallow enough to avoid introducing heavy subsurface plasticity but deep enough to serve as a reliable stress concentrator. Futagami and Akashi's observation that the crack front can deviate from the nominal loading direction (pqac-00000020) underscores that even with a guide notch, the cleavage path is not guaranteed to be perfectly straight, particularly in crystals with high grown-in dislocation densities or sub-grain structure.

---

### Summary of Practical Recommendations

For cleaving a 10 × 10 × 10 mm MgO single crystal along {100} at room temperature in air:

1. Use a fresh, sharp single-edge razor blade or fine-edged chisel.
2. Place the crystal on a compliant pad (tissue paper or soft polymer mat).
3. Align the blade edge precisely along a ⟨100⟩ direction on the target {100} face.
4. Optionally pre-score lightly with a diamond scribe along the intended cleavage line to guide initiation.
5. Apply a single, light, sharp tap with a small hammer.
6. Splitting approximately in half is more reliable than attempting thin slabs; slabs thinner than ~1 mm become increasingly difficult.
7. Remove loose debris by blowing with dry nitrogen or compressed air (pqac-00000041).

The method is broadly reliable for MgO given its low cleavage toughness (0.81 MPa·m^(1/2)) and perfect {100} cleavage, but the user should expect occasional cleavage steps, river lines, and minor surface damage, particularly if the blade is dull, the crystal contains sub-grain boundaries, or the impact force is excessive."}

## Cleavage of Bulk Single-Crystal MgO Along {100}: Techniques, Reliability, Failure Modes, and Quantitative Properties

### Background

Magnesium oxide (MgO, periclase) crystallizes in the NaCl-type rock-salt structure (space group Fm3̅m), which provides three mutually perpendicular families of {100} cleavage planes (langdon1968mechanicalbehaviorof pages 1-8, schultz1994singlecrystalcleavage pages 1-3). Because each {100} plane is electrostatically neutral—alternating cations and anions across the surface—it satisfies the charge-neutrality exclusionary criterion for cleavage in ionic crystals, whereas {111} planes are non-neutral and cannot cleave (schultz1994singlecrystalcleavage pages 6-9). The {100} cleavage toughness of MgO is 0.81 MPa·m^(1/2), derived from Gilman's (1960) measurements and tabulated by Schultz, Jensen, and Bradt (1994) among other cubic structures (schultz1994singlecrystalcleavage pages 11-13). This is roughly three times larger than the cleavage toughness of softer halide crystals such as KBr (0.12 MPa·m^(1/2)) or NaCl (0.17 MPa·m^(1/2)), but still well below 1 MPa·m^(1/2) and therefore in the regime where cleavage proceeds readily once an adequate crack is initiated (schultz1994singlecrystalcleavage pages 13-15).

The following table summarizes the key quantitative properties governing {100} cleavage of single-crystal MgO:

| Property | Value / description | Relevance to cleavage | Source |
|---|---:|---|---|
| Crystal structure | Rock-salt (NaCl type), space group Fm3̅m | Cubic symmetry provides three mutually perpendicular {100} cleavage-plane families. | (langdon1968mechanicalbehaviorof pages 1-8, schultz1994singlecrystalcleavage pages 13-15, boffi1976onthecleavage pages 1-5) |
| Preferred cleavage plane | {100} | (100), (010), and (001) are symmetry-equivalent, readily cleaved planes. | (amodeo2018dislocationsandplastic pages 17-19, schultz1994singlecrystalcleavage pages 13-15, jandacka2011fractureenergyof pages 1-2) |
| {100} cleavage toughness, Kᵢc | 0.81 MPa·m¹ᐟ² | Indicates brittle, rapid crack propagation once a suitable flaw is initiated. | (schultz1994singlecrystalcleavage pages 11-13) |
| {100} surface energy—Gilman | 1.20 J·m⁻² = 1200 erg·cm⁻² | Experimental monocrystal-cleavage value; reported repeatability was approximately 15% for three measurements. | (jandacka2011fractureenergyof pages 4-5, boffi1976onthecleavage pages 5-8, jandacka2011fractureenergyof media f70adc15) |
| {100} surface energy—Westwood and Goldheim | Approximately 1.04–1.15 J·m⁻² = 1040–1150 erg·cm⁻² | Independent experimental range supporting a cleavage-surface energy near 1 J·m⁻². | (boffi1976onthecleavage pages 5-8) |
| Literature-average {100} surface energy | 1.26 J·m⁻² | Average of published values excluding an outlier; useful as a representative value for fresh {100} cleavage. | (jandacka2011fractureenergyof pages 5-7, jandacka2011fractureenergyof media f70adc15) |
| Calculated {100} surface energy | 0.89 J·m⁻² = 890 erg·cm⁻² | Boffi–Ricci lattice-dynamical result; markedly below their calculated (110) value of 2.591 J·m⁻². | (boffi1976onthecleavage pages 5-8) |
| Random-particle fracture energy | 2.37 J·m⁻² | Includes surface creation and dissipative work and may sample planes other than {100}; it is not the ideal {100} surface energy. | (jandacka2011fractureenergyof pages 4-5, jandacka2011fractureenergyof media f70adc15) |
| Random-particle measured surface energy | 1.79 J·m⁻² | Higher than the {100} literature average because randomly oriented cracks may include higher-energy planes such as {110}. | (jandacka2011fractureenergyof pages 4-5, jandacka2011fractureenergyof pages 5-7) |
| Mohs hardness | 5.5 | MgO can damage or blunt an ordinary steel edge, reinforcing the need for a fresh, sharp blade. | (jandacka2011fractureenergyof pages 2-4) |
| Knoop hardness on cleaved {100}, indenter aligned with ⟨100⟩ | Approximately 11.0 ± 0.5 GPa | Demonstrates substantial penetration resistance and indentation anisotropy despite low cleavage toughness. | (everitt1990indentationcreepand pages 74-81) |
| Shallow nanoindentation hardness | Up to 35 GPa at approximately 40 nm depth | Strong indentation-size and tip-geometry effects make this unsuitable as a bulk hardness value. | (nazarov2003nanoindentationmicroindentationand pages 3-5, nazarov2003nanoindentationmicroindentationand pages 5-7) |

contexts.context: The excerpt describes mechanical impact cleavage, not a razor-blade or wedge procedure. MgO single-crystal blocks approximately 7 × 7 × 7 mm³ were cleaved at room temperature into specimens about 1 mm thick using a chisel fitted with a sharp knife edge. The chisel was positioned on the (010) face, with its knife edge aligned along [001]. A blow was then applied to the chisel in the [010] direction, producing a cleavage crack on the (100) plane. This is one member of the {100} cleavage family; changing the crystallographic orientation would give the equivalent symmetry-related {100} planes. The crack was generated by a rapid impact, and the authors note that the resulting cleavage-crack speed should be very high. Thus, the practical tool was a sharp-edged chisel—effectively a wedge-like cutting edge driven by impact—rather than a loose razor blade. The specimen preparation was performed at room temperature, although MgO is reported to cleave well along {100} planes even at relatively high temperatures.

contexts.context: The excerpt is relevant to the cleavage surface energy of MgO, but it does not provide numerical values for the fracture toughness K_Ic, cleavage surface energy, hardness, or cleavage toughness on {100}. Instead, it presents a theoretical phase-transition model for cleavage. Under applied stress, MgO is considered to become unstable when the separation of atomic planes reaches a critical displacement. The model separates the energy into a reversible contribution, γc, representing the work per unit area required to reach the critical configuration, and an additional irreversible contribution, γb, needed for complete separation into two free surfaces. For the easy [100] cleavage direction, the critical displacement and γc are related to the mean-square atomic displacement at the melting temperature, with an anisotropy factor B approximately equal to 1.1. A further contribution is estimated using the difference between boiling and melting temperatures. Numerical material-property values and any explicit {100} cleavage-toughness value are absent from the supplied pages.

contexts.context: The excerpt links poor or failed cleavage in MgO primarily to localized plastic deformation generated during crack propagation. Concentrated stress at the crack tip nucleates fresh dislocations rather than merely mobilizing pre-existing grown-in dislocations. These dislocations form long, parallel arrays near major cleavage steps, lie close to and parallel with the cleaved surface, and are identified as edge dislocations from their Burgers vectors. contexts.context: The excerpt indicates that poor or failed cleavage in MgO is chiefly associated with competition between the energy required to create new cleavage surfaces and energy dissipated through plastic deformation. As a crack advances, its stress field can produce resolved shear stress on (110) planes for dislocations having a 1/2<110>-type Burgers vector, allowing dislocation slip ahead of the crack. When crack speed reaches about 1% of the sound velocity, plastic work is predicted to occur suddenly; dislocation motion then consumes energy and increases the effective surface energy. The calculated plastic-work contribution is generally only several percent of MgO’s intrinsic surface energy at room temperature, so plasticity usually has a limited effect. However, changes in crack velocity can make this contribution significant and may therefore promote unstable, slowed, or otherwise ineffective cleavage. The excerpt also describes dislocation-loop behavior: smaller loops escape to the surface through the imaging force, while larger loops are dragged into the crystal, producing a measurable penetration depth. It does not provide specific evidence in this passage for cleavage steps, crack deflection, or subgrain-boundary effects; those mechanisms would require additional sections of the article. Because MgO has a NaCl-type ionic structure, it can undergo plastic deformation rather than separating immediately by fracture. The principal easy-slip system is {110}<110>, with glide occurring in the <110> direction; at elevated temperatures, {100}<110> glide can also become active. contexts.context: The excerpt indicates that poor or failed cleavage in MgO is strongly controlled by plastic deformation and the density and distribution of dislocations and slip bands. Stroh cracks can form from dislocation pile-ups against kink bands and occur on conjugate {110} slip planes rather than the normal {100} cleavage planes. Uniform slip across an entire plane is energetically impossible; plastic flow instead occurs through mobile dislocations. contexts.context: The excerpt indicates that pre-scoring, indentation pre-cracking, or sawing a guide notch generally helps initiate cleavage on a selected crystallographic plane rather than hurting cleavage initiation. These methods are used experimentally to force the incipient crack to start on the plane of interest, especially when measuring cleavage or fracture toughness. The notch does not necessarily determine the long-term fracture path: after propagating only a short distance, a crack in a single crystal is redirected by the crystal structure onto its preferred cleavage plane. Thus, for MgO or other ionic crystals, a guide notch should be understood primarily as an initiation aid and plane-selection tool, not as the fundamental cause of cleavage. The excerpt does not provide MgO-specific data, but it explicitly concludes from ionic crystal results, including LiF, that fracture toughness (cleavage toughness) is the appropriate cleavage criterion. It also notes that cleavage-plane toughness is often the lowest among tested planes. Any conclusions about whether sawing damage quantitatively lowers initiation resistance, or about MgO’s specific response, would require additional MgO-specific evidence not included here.

It does, however, show that cleavage was initiated by an applied impact and that crack-tip stress concentration produced newly nucleated edge dislocations during fracture. This supports the general rationale for using a sharp, controlled notch or score as a cleavage guide: it can concentrate stress and establish a preferred fracture origin. The observations also caution that the crack may not follow the nominal loading direction; in one MgO specimen, the cleavage front deviated from [010] toward [01T]. contexts.context: The excerpt indicates that introducing a notch, score, saw mark, or other surface damage would generally promote cleavage initiation in MgO by providing a pre-existing flaw from which fracture can develop. Damaged or cleaved surfaces produced fracture origins at the crystal periphery, coincident with surface flaws. Even edge micro-cracks smaller than the critical Griffith size could grow once slip occurred and lead to fracture. Conversely, polishing away such cracks increased ductility five- to tenfold, while polished crystals fractured through the dynamic interaction of orthogonal slip bands rather than from an obvious surface flaw. Thus, a deliberately introduced notch would likely reduce the stress or deformation required to initiate cleavage, although the excerpt does not provide a controlled comparison of scored, sawn, and unnotched specimens or quantify notch geometry effects. The passage also emphasizes that crack growth—not merely nucleation—is critical: slip-band density and distribution can restrict micro-crack growth and produce stable narrow slits instead of immediate catastrophic failure. Therefore, a notch may assist initiation but its ultimate effect depends on surface condition, slip activity, crack geometry, and whether surrounding plastic deformation arrests or accelerates the crack.

It does establish that MgO has the halite-type cubic structure and cleaves on the {100} planes. Ionic crystals with cubic cleavage generally have relatively low cleavage toughnesses, mostly below 1 MPa m^1/2, so once a suitable crack is initiated, cleavage can be comparatively easy. However, MgO is grouped with LiF as having a higher cleavage toughness than KBr and PbS—about three times higher—because of its smaller ions and higher elastic modulus. The article attributes higher toughness to more tightly bonded, stiffer ionic structures. Thus, based on this excerpt alone, a notch would likely be relevant as a stress concentrator for initiating cleavage, but the text gives no evidence that pre-scoring specifically improves cleavage, reduces the required force, or produces a preferred propagation path. For MgO, any guided notch should be aligned with the {100} cleavage orientation, while recognizing that its stronger ionic bonding may make initiation more demanding than in softer, more weakly bonded ionic crystals. contexts.context: The excerpt provides general context for cleavage in ionic and covalently bonded crystals, but it does not directly discuss whether pre-scoring, sawing, or machining a notch helps or hinders cleavage initiation in MgO or other ionic crystals. It emphasizes that cleavage is fundamentally the rupture of bonds between atoms or ions, so the relevant criterion must be connected to bonding and charge arrangement. In ionic crystals, cleavage planes must also produce compatible, matching fracture surfaces; planes that leave all positive charges on one face and all negative charges on the other are described as non-neutral and are not expected to cleave in the simple manner discussed. The article further argues that no universal crystallographic rule—such as unit-cell bounding planes or most closely packed planes—determines cleavage for all materials, and that crystal properties are more informative than structure alone. Thus, the passage may support considering how a notch interacts with bond strength, charge neutrality, and the selected crystallographic plane, but it supplies no experimental evidence about notch-induced cleavage initiation, notch sharpness, sawing damage, or MgO specifically.

contexts.context: The excerpt does not discuss MgO, room-temperature cleaving, vendor procedures, tools, support, scoring, or cube reliability. It provides only general context: complex/covalent crystals tend to have higher cleavage toughness than simple ionic crystals; a conservative upper estimate for brittle single-crystal cleavage toughness is about “5 MPa m^1/2,” based on diamond and sapphire. It notes polycrystalline toughness commonly exceeds single-crystal cleavage by only roughly 1–2 MPa m^1/2, with values of 1.8–2.0 MPa m^1/2 for polycrystalline spinel and 1.6–3.6 MPa m^1/2 for fluorite.
contexts.question: How is bulk single-crystal MgO (periclase, rock-salt structure) cleaved along {100} at room temperature in air, and how reliable is it for a 10 x 10 x 10 mm cube? (1) Does placing a single-edge razor blade or chisel on a {100} face parallel to a cube edge and tapping it with a small hammer reliably produce a {100} cleavage, as the crystal vendor SPI Supplies describes in its note 'Cleaving and Polishing MgO Crystal Substrates'? (2) What tool (razor blade, knife edge, chisel, wedge), impact (light tap vs. sharp blow, hammer mass), support (hard anvil vs. compliant mat), and geometry (splitting the crystal in half vs. taking a thin slab near an edge; minimum slab thickness) are recommended? (3) What are the documented causes of failed or poor cleaves in MgO, e.g., dull blade, plastic deformation and dislocation slip on {110}<1-10> under the blade, subgrain boundaries, impurities, crack deflection, chipping, cleavage steps? (4) Does pre-scoring or sawing a notch help or hurt cleavage initiation in MgO? Cite primary literature (e.g., Gilman's cleavage experiments; Stokes, Johnston and Li; Westwood) and vendor or laboratory procedures where available, and give quantitative values (fracture toughness, {100} cleavage surface energy, hardness) where possible.

contexts.context: The excerpt discusses MgO in the context of cubic cleavage in ionic crystals with the NaCl structure. MgO cleaves on {100}, and its cleavage toughness is grouped with LiF as being approximately three times greater than the values for KBr and PbS. The text attributes this trend to MgO and LiF having smaller ions, stronger bonding, and higher elastic moduli than the compounds containing larger, more polarizable ions. It does not provide an explicit numerical MgO K_Ic value in the supplied pages, although it states that cubic-cleavage toughnesses are generally below 1 MPa m^1/2, with some approaching approximately 1 MPa m^1/2. The excerpt does not report MgO’s {100} surface energy, nor does it provide a hardness value for MgO single crystal. It also distinguishes MgO from pyrite and spinel, which have higher cubic-cleavage toughnesses of about 1 MPa m^1/2. Thus, the passage supports qualitative interpretation of MgO’s cleavage toughness and bonding-related trends, but numerical fracture toughness, surface-energy, and hardness values would need to be obtained from the article’s tables or other sources.

contexts.context: The excerpt concerns the theoretical cleavage energy and surface-energy framework for MgO, rather than reporting MgO fracture-toughness (KIc), hardness, or clearly tabulated numerical cleavage-energy values. Cleavage is modeled as a stress-induced phase transition: under uniaxial stress, the perfect lattice becomes unstable when the separation of planes reaches a critical displacement. The reversible work per unit area needed to reach this unstable configuration is denoted by γc, while an additional contribution γb is required for complete irreversible separation into two free surfaces. The model relates the critical displacement and cleavage work to interplanar force constants, phonon eigenfrequencies/eigenvectors, and a direction-dependent factor B(hkl). The [100] orientation is identified as the easy cleavage direction, and the text indicates anisotropy for other orientations, including [110]. MgO has the NaCl crystal structure and is treated using a modified breathing-shell model based on its elastic and phonon properties. However, the supplied pages do not provide a numerical value for KIc, a numerical {100} surface energy, or a hardness value for MgO single crystals. They also do not give the final numerical results, which appear to be discussed later in the article.

contexts.context: The excerpt provides only comparative information about MgO, not the requested numerical MgO values for fracture toughness, {100} cleavage-plane surface energy, or single-crystal hardness. It states that Gilman’s theory predicts a {110}/{100} fracture-toughness ratio of approximately 1.8 for MgO, compared with 1.3–1.4 for MgAl2O4. MgO is described as having the same primary {100} and secondary {110} cleavage planes as MgAl2O4, with a similar Young’s modulus but somewhat lower elastic anisotropy. The discussion also notes that, unlike MgAl2O4, MgO generally exhibits macroscopic fracture on the {100} plane rather than the secondary {110} plane, because {110} apparently has higher fracture toughness. Crack branching can occur from the higher-toughness {110} plane onto the lower-toughness {100} plane in MgO. These points may help contextualize MgO cleavage behavior and relative toughness, but the excerpt does not report MgO’s absolute KIc values, the surface energy of the {100} cleavage plane, or hardness measurements.

contexts.context: The excerpt does not give an absolute fracture-toughness (KIc) value for MgO single crystals, nor does it report Vickers or Mohs hardness for MgO. MgO is discussed only comparatively. The cited theoretical work predicts a {110}/{100} KIc ratio of approximately 1.8 for MgO, higher than the predicted 1.3–1.4 ratio for MgAl2O4. The text also states that MgO has {100} as its primary cleavage plane and {110} as its secondary cleavage plane, with the {110} plane having higher KIc; consequently, macroscopic fracture in MgO is generally observed on {100}, unlike the closer competition between {100} and {110} fracture in MgAl2O4. The numerical KIc values actually reported in the excerpt—approximately 0.9–1.0 MPa·m^1/2 from fractography, with adjusted averages around 1.21 and 1.28 MPa·m^1/2—are for stoichiometric MgAl2O4, not MgO. Therefore, the requested MgO absolute KIc and hardness values would need to be obtained from another source or a different portion of the cited literature.

contexts.context: The excerpt does not specifically describe using a razor blade; it describes a sharp knife-edged chisel, so a razor-blade procedure would be an adaptation of this method rather than a directly reported protocol. The MgO crystals were approximately 7 × 7 × 7 mm³ and were cleaved at room temperature into specimens about 1 mm thick. For the reported orientation, the chisel’s knife edge was aligned along [001] and positioned on the (010) face; a blow was then applied in the [010] direction. contexts.context: The excerpt reports nanoindentation hardness measurements for MgO using a Berkovich indenter. Hardness was calculated from the applied load divided by the projected contact area after correcting displacement data for elastic deflection. The hardness varies strongly with indentation depth: it increases slowly between approximately 800 and 300 nm, then rises sharply below 300 nm, reaching a reported value of 35 GPa at a depth of 40 nm. The authors attribute this apparent high hardness primarily to the indenter-tip geometry and indentation-size effects rather than necessarily to a load-dependent intrinsic mechanical property. Real indenters have a spherical or chisel-edge imperfection, and for hard materials this defect becomes comparable to the contact size at low loads. For the Berkovich indenter, the tip defect is stated to be approximately 40 nm, and loads below 10 mN can therefore produce considerable hardness values. The provided excerpt does not give separate numerical Vickers or Knoop hardness values, nor does it explicitly state the crystallographic surface as {100}; it only provides the depth-dependent nanoindentation result for MgO.
